The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Mediterranean sand smelt (Atherina hepsetus) was determined during the peak spawning period, yielding a value of 9.18% [GSI = 9.18%] under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This relatively modest index suggests that reproductive investment per spawning event is moderate compared to some other atherinids, though it aligns well with the iteroparous strategy typical of small coastal teleosts. Newly fertilised eggs, which are demersal and adhesive, have a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams] based on the average egg diameter of approximately 1 millimetre. The incubation period under the same thermal regime of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] is brief, with the age at birth recorded as 26 days [ab = 26 days] from fertilisation. During this yolk-sac larval phase, the developing embryo relies entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding after eclosion, a critical transition that determines early survival rates in the planktonic environment.

Field surveys and otolith-based back-calculation have provided robust estimates of maximum body size for this species. The ultimate total length reaches 20 centimetres [Li = 20 centimetres], a value characteristic of a medium-sized silverside within the genus Atherina. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight is calculated at 55.9 grams [Wwi = 55.9 grams] using the length-weight relationship derived from mature specimens. These asymptotic dimensions are attained over a relatively extended growing period, reflecting the moderate growth rates typical of fish inhabiting warm-temperate coastal lagoons. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Atherina presbyter suggest that the Mediterranean sand smelt achieves a slightly smaller maximum size, possibly in response to the more confined and variable conditions of its preferred shallow-water habitats. Juvenile fish undergoing the larval-juvenile transition exhibit rapid increases in both length and mass, though the allometric shift associated with metamorphosis moderates the rate of somatic expansion as individuals approach adulthood.

Sexual maturation in Mediterranean sand smelt is characterised by a well-defined total length at puberty of 6.5 centimetres [Lp = 6.5 centimetres], a threshold derived from histological examination of gonad development in field-collected juveniles. At this size, individuals have attained a wet weight at puberty of 1.75 grams [Wwp = 1.75 grams], representing a substantial increase from the birth mass. The timing of this developmental milestone is closely linked to water temperature, and under the consistent thermal conditions of 19 °C [T = 19 °C] that dominate the summer growing season, the time since birth at puberty is estimated at 365 days [tp = 365 days]. This interval corresponds to approximately one calendar year, aligning with an annual reproductive cycle in which young-of-the-year fish mature during their second spring. The onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation follows shortly after this length threshold is crossed, ensuring that first spawning coincides with favourable environmental conditions for larval survival.

Longevity records for this species indicate a maximum lifespan of 1825 days [am = 1825 days], equivalent to approximately five years under natural conditions when measured at the prevailing water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This duration is typical for small-bodied coastal fishes, though some individuals in particularly stable lagoon environments may approach this upper limit. The life history strategy emphasises repeated spawning events across multiple seasons, with adults investing in somatic maintenance between reproductive bouts. Reproductive senescence has not been systematically documented, but age-related declines in fecundity are suspected in the oldest cohort. Field observations of tagged individuals suggest that mortality rates increase sharply after the fourth year, driven by predation pressure and the energetic costs of successive spawning seasons. The interplay between lifespan and reproductive output is therefore a critical determinant of population dynamics in this species.

The reproductive strategy of Atherina hepsetus is characterised by multiple spawning events within each breeding season. Gravid females produce clutches of demersal eggs, and the fecundity per reproductive event is estimated at approximately 1000 eggs per spawning [N_R_i = approximately 1000 eggs per spawning], based on counts of hydrated oocytes in ripe ovaries. The frequency of these events is high, with individuals spawning up to 1.5 times annually [F_R_i = up to 1.5 times annually] under favourable thermal and trophic conditions. This iteroparous pattern, in which a single female can release several thousand eggs across a breeding season, buffers the population against stochastic variations in early-life survival.
